source_text: Non enim in uetere testamento tantum scriptum est: ego facio bona et condo mala, sed euidentius in nouo, ubi dominus dicit: nolite timere eos, qui corpus occidunt et amplius non habent, quid faciant, sed eum timete, qui cum corpus occiderit, habet potestatem animam mittere in gehennam. uoluntariae autem corruptioni addi iudicio diuino poenalem corruptionem manifestissime apostolus Paulus adtestatur, cum dicit: templum enim dei . sanctum est, quod estis uos; quisquis templum dei corruperit, corrumpet illum deus. quod si in uetere lege dictum esset, quibus inuectionibus isti inpetum facerent accusantes quasi corruptorem deum! quod uerbum metuentes multi latini interpretes noluerunt dicere „corrUmpet,M sed dixerunt "disperdet" illum deus, et non deuiantes a re ipsa offensionem uocabuli deuitarunt. quamquam isti non minus inueherentur in perditorem deum, si hoc in lege uetere aut prophetis inuenirent. sed graecis exemplaribus conuincuntur, in quibus apertissime scriptum est: quisquis templum dei corruperit. corrumpet illum deus. quod si quis ab eis quaerat quomodo dictum sit, ne corruptor putetur deus, exponunt statim "corrumpet" dictum esse: corruptioni tradet, uel si quo alio modo possunt. quo animo si essent in ueterem legem, et multa ibi miranda intellegerent et nondum intellecta non cum odio lacerarent, sed cum honore differrent.
orientation: Augustine is arguing that God justly adds penal corruption to voluntary corruption, and he defends the wording of 1 Corinthians 3:17 against Manichaean objections.
pass_a_gloss: For not only in the Old Testament is it written: I make good things and create evils, but more clearly in the New, where the Lord says: do not fear those who kill the body and have nothing more that they can do, but fear him who, when he has killed the body, has power to send the soul into Gehenna. But that penal corruption is added to voluntary corruption by divine judgment, the apostle Paul most clearly attests, when he says: for the temple of God is holy, which you are; whoever corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt him. But if this had been said in the old law, with what invectives would they make an attack, accusing God as if a corrupter! Fearing this word, many Latin translators did not want to say 'corrumpet,' but said 'disperdet'—God will destroy him—and, not deviating from the thing itself, they avoided the offense of the word. Although they would inveigh no less against God as a destroyer, if they found this in the old law or in the prophets. But they are refuted by the Greek copies, in which it is most openly written: whoever corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt him. But if someone asks them how it was said, lest God be thought a corrupter, they immediately explain that 'corrumpet' was said for 'he will hand over to corruption,' or in whatever other way they can. If they had this disposition toward the old law, they would both understand many things there that are to be wondered at, and they would not tear apart things not yet understood with hatred, but would defer them with honor.

choices.why: The verb condo means to found or establish; 'create' fits the divine act and matches the Old Testament quotation's sense of God as source of both good and evil outcomes.
The adjective poenalis means 'of or belonging to punishment'; 'penal' is the precise English equivalent and preserves the legal/judicial force Augustine intends.
This is the literal rendering Augustine insists on from the Greek, and the whole passage turns on the shocking force of 'corrupt' applied to God's action.
The Latin translators' softening word disperdo means to scatter or utterly destroy; 'destroy' captures their avoidance of 'corrupt.'

choices.english: he will hand over to corruption
choices.why: The phrase tradere + dative means to deliver or hand over to a power or state; this is the explanatory paraphrase Augustine reports.
Differre here means to postpone or set aside for later consideration; 'defer with honor' captures the respectful suspension of judgment Augustine contrasts with their hatred.

pass_b_english: For it is not only in the Old Testament that it is written, “I make good things and create evils” (Isaiah 45:7), but even more clearly in the New, where the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body and after that have nothing more they can do; but fear him who, after he has killed the body, has power to send the soul into hell” (Luke 12:4-5). And the apostle Paul bears the clearest witness that penal corruption is added to voluntary corruption by divine judgment, when he says: “For the temple of God is holy, and that temple you are; whoever corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt him” (1 Corinthians 3:17). If this had been said in the old law, what attacks they would make, accusing God as a corrupter! Fearing that word, many Latin translators refused to say “God will corrupt him,” but said “God will destroy him,” and without departing from the reality they avoided the offense of the word. Yet these people would inveigh no less against God as a destroyer if they found this in the old law or the prophets. But they are refuted by the Greek copies, in which it is written most plainly: “Whoever corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt him.” And if someone asks them how this is said, so that God is not thought a corrupter, they immediately explain that “he will corrupt” means “he will hand over to corruption,” or whatever other way they can. If they had this attitude toward the old law, they would understand many things there that are worthy of wonder, and things not yet understood they would not tear apart with hatred, but would defer them with honor.

problems.source_quote: nolite timere eos, qui corpus occidunt et amplius non habent, quid faciant, sed eum timete, qui cum corpus occiderit, habet potestatem animam mittere in gehennam
problems.why: The quotation matches Luke 12:4-5, not Matthew 10:28. Matthew has 'fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.' Luke has 'kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do... hath power to cast into hell.' The source quote follows Luke's wording.
problems.ruling: Source 'amplius non habent quid faciant' matches Luke 12:4-5, not Matthew 10:28.

fixed: Changed citation from Matthew 10:28 to Luke 12:4-5: the source wording 'nolite timere eos, qui corpus occidunt et amplius non habent, quid faciant, sed eum timete, qui cum corpus occiderit, habet potestatem animam mittere in gehennam' matches Luke 12:4-5, not Matthew 10:28.
